text: Large language models frequently produce fluent but factually incorrect statements, a failure mode commonly referred to as hallucination. Prior work attributes this behaviour to the parametric nature of the knowledge stored in model weights, which cannot be inspected or updated after pre-training. We argue that grounding generation in retrieved documents addresses the root cause rather than the symptom, because the model is no longer required to recall facts from its parameters alone.
title: Grounding Language Model Generation in Retrieved Evidence

text: We evaluate retrieval-augmented generation against a closed-book baseline on the FactCheck-QA benchmark. Retrieval-augmented generation reduces the hallucination rate from 31.2% to 14.4%, a relative reduction of 53.8%. The improvement is consistent across all three model scales we tested, and the gap widens as the questions require more specialised domain knowledge. We report the mean over five random seeds; the standard deviation of the hallucination rate is below 0.8 percentage points in every configuration.
title: Grounding Language Model Generation in Retrieved Evidence

text: Retrieval quality bounds the benefit of grounding. When the retriever fails to surface the gold passage, the generator hallucinates at roughly the same rate as the closed-book baseline. This observation motivates a second stage of reranking: a cross-encoder rescores the candidates returned by the dense retriever and promotes the passage that actually answers the question. Adding a cross-encoder reranker raises answer accuracy by a further 6.1 points on FactCheck-QA.
title: Grounding Language Model Generation in Retrieved Evidence

text: Cross-lingual retrieval poses a distinct challenge: the query and the corpus are written in different languages, so lexical overlap is essentially zero. Dense multilingual encoders map both languages into a shared embedding space, but we find that the resulting similarity scores are poorly calibrated across language pairs. A multilingual cross-encoder reranker recovers most of the loss, improving nDCG@10 by 11.3 points over dense retrieval alone on our Chinese-to-English evaluation set.
title: Calibrated Reranking for Cross-Lingual Evidence Retrieval

text: We ablate the reranking stage to quantify its contribution. Removing the cross-encoder drops precision@5 from 0.71 to 0.48 in the Chinese-to-English setting, whereas the same ablation in the monolingual English setting costs only 0.09. The asymmetry indicates that reranking matters substantially more when the query language differs from the document language. We therefore recommend treating the reranker as mandatory rather than optional in cross-lingual pipelines.
title: Calibrated Reranking for Cross-Lingual Evidence Retrieval

text: Threshold selection governs when an agentic retrieval loop should terminate. We adopt a two-sided rule over the reranker score: if any passage exceeds the upper threshold the claim is treated as supported and retrieval halts immediately, while if every candidate falls below the lower threshold the corpus is deemed to lack coverage and further querying is abandoned. Claims whose best score lands between the two thresholds trigger one additional reformulated query. This rule cuts the average number of retrieval rounds from 4.6 to 2.3 without measurable loss in evidence recall.
title: Calibrated Reranking for Cross-Lingual Evidence Retrieval
